chunks: Saad narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from al-Qasim ibn 'Urwah, from 'Abdullah ibn Bukayr, from Zurarah, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:
"There is no harm in praying behind the Nāsib (one who opposes the Imams), and you should not recite behind him in what he recites audibly, for his recitation suffices for you when you hear it."

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: This report is attributed to the state of Taqiyya (prudence/concealment), and it is possible that he meant: Do not recite a recitation that you make audible just as the Imam makes audible, and rather it is permissible for him to recite what is between him and himself (silently).

key_terms.التَّقِيَّةِ: Taqiyya; the practice of concealing one's faith or beliefs out of fear of persecution, often cited to explain apparent contradictions in hadith.
key_terms.النَّاصِبِ: Nāsib; one who opposes or is hostile to the Imams, specifically used in Shia jurisprudence for those who reject the Wilayah of Ali (AS).
key_terms.تُجْزِيكَ: Tujzīka; it suffices for you; it fulfills the obligation of recitation.
key_terms.يَجْهَرُ: Yajharu; to recite audibly (Jahr), as opposed to silently (Ikhfa).

ai.seo_question: Can I pray behind an Imam who opposes the Ahl al-Bayt, and do I need to recite Surah al-Fatihah?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the fiqh of praying behind a *Nāsib* (one opposed to the Ahl al-Bayt), ruling that the follower's audible recitation is not required as the Imam's recitation suffices. Shaykh al-Tusi notes that this may be a ruling of *Taqiyya* (prudence) to avoid conflict, or simply that the follower recites silently (*Ikhfat*) while the Imam recites aloud (*Jahr*). This highlights the flexibility in Shia jurisprudence regarding the validity of congregational prayer even with those of differing theological standing.
